10898-american-scenes-and-christian-slav:
Ebenezer Davies, a minister lately of Berbice in Guiana, toured more than four thousand miles of the United States in the 1840s and published this account in 1849. Entering at New Orleans, he travelled north to Boston and west to Utica, watching slavery at close hand as a British abolitionist and a pastor whose own congregation included formerly enslaved people.

Davies describes Southern plantations, Northern churches, and the growth of Puritan principles in New England, praising what he admires and denouncing what he finds cruel. He also notes American expansion and the talk of annexation. The book gives a foreign visitor's view of the republic on the eve of its great sectional crisis, sharp on slavery and curious about everything else.
10989-our-saviour:
Father Tuck's New Testament series presents the life of Jesus for children in this short illustrated book. The story begins at Nazareth, where Jesus lives quietly until John the Baptist preaches and baptises in the Jordan. John says one greater will come, then baptises Jesus himself, despite feeling unworthy, and the Spirit descends like a dove as a voice calls Jesus the beloved Son.

Forty days of temptation in the wilderness follow, then preaching by the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus calls fishermen as disciples. Later scenes show special kindness to little children, whom the disciples would turn away, and a child set among disputing disciples to teach humility. Simple language and pictures make the Gospel story accessible to young readers.
11085-m-or-n-similia-similibus-curantur:
G. J. Whyte-Melville wrote this Victorian novel of society, crime, and love, titled M. or N. and subtitled Similia similibus curantur, like cures like. A wild wet night in the Channel opens the story, with cross-seas off Calais, a French sentry humming opera, and a Queen's Messenger sick on the mail packet. Tom Ryfe, Gentleman Jim, Dick Stanmore, and Nina carry the plot through thirty chapters.

Cracksmen, officers' messes, missing gentlemen and wanted ladies, and a coming queen mix with balls, tea-rooms, and partings. Dick watches a lady with another man in a deserted tea-room and knows his first misfortune has come. Whyte-Melville, known for hunting novels, writes here a tale of London and country society, with rogues and lovers crossing paths.
11266-sonnets-by-the-nawab-nizamat-jung-:
This 1917 sonnet sequence by the Nawab Nizamat Jung Bahadur, privately printed in Madras in 1914, gathers twenty-four sonnets on love in its highest sense. from Rebirth and Before the Throne through Love's Silence, Eternal Joy, and Two Hearts in One, with a prologue and epilogue. Epigraphs from Empedocles and Plato frame love as nourishment for the soul's wings. A foreword by R. C. Fraser introduces the author.

Born in Hyderabad and educated in England, the Nawab wrote during rare leisure in a busy public life, and Fraser notes his popular war lyric India to England. A note on the sonnet's history in English literature accompanies the poems. The volume offers a distinctive meeting of Indian devotion and English form.
12588-cavour:
Countess Evelyn Martinengo-Cesaresco's 1898 life of Cavour traces the statesman who made modern Italy. Chapters move from heredity and environment through travel years, journalism and parliament to the great ministry. The Crimean War, the Congress of Paris, the pact of Plombières, the war of 1859, Savoy and Nice, the Sicilian expedition and the kingdom of Italy follow.

Cavour, the book argues, worked by evolution, not catastrophe, though change often looks like leaps and bounds. Rome voted capital closes the story. Martinengo-Cesaresco writes as an admiring biographer, clear on diplomacy and character. The life remains a readable English portrait of Italian unification, centred on its ablest minister.
13193-supreme-personality-fun-in-living-:
Dr. Delmer Eugene Croft's Supreme Personality, subtitled Fun in Living, is a twenty-five-cent cure for doubt, fear, and worry, in its hundredth thousand printing. Croft promises that a reader can grow grander and handsomer at eighty than at eighteen, if the spiritual, mental, and physical cash register stays in order. Thought waves, he claims, can heal, guide, and build personal power.

Pages give exercises for breath and muscle, urging deep abdominal breaths through the nose and forceful release through the mouth, never holding the breath. Croft cites Vanderbilt adding millions after eighty, Wordsworth winning the laureateship at seventy-three, and Verdi writing Falstaff late in life. The booklet is cheerful, brash self-help from the age of mind power.
13433-a-reply-to-dr-lightfoot-s-essays-b:
Walter R. Cassels, writing anonymously in 1889 as the author of Supernatural Religion, answers Bishop Lightfoot's essays on his work. He opens by welcoming Lightfoot's recovery from illness, then turns to the hard question at issue: whether early Christian writings can be shown genuine, and what their silence proves.

Cassels argues that epistles whose authenticity is so hard to establish cannot carry great weight, and he tests claims that Polycarp quotes the Gospels. Point by point, footnote by footnote, he states the case for sceptics in its strongest form before answering it. The book is a dense Victorian debate over dates, texts, and the roots of Christian belief.
14072-primitive-christian-worship-or-the:
J. Endell Tyler, rector of Saint Giles-in-the-Fields, published this second edition in 1847 against the invocation of saints, angels, and the Virgin Mary. Scripture and church history supply his evidence, and his preface pleads for less hostility between Roman Catholics and Anglicans. Prove all things and hold fast what is good stands as his motto.

Close reading carries the case. Tyler tests patristic quotations, exposing one prayer wrongly credited to Origen on the Lamentations. He then turns to Luke, where the boy Jesus tells his parents he must be about his Father's business, and to the wedding at Cana. Neither passage, he argues, grants Mary divine honor. Long, learned, and partisan, the book remains a clear record of Victorian church controversy fought with footnotes.
14878-the-relation-of-the-hro-lfs-saga-k:
Oscar Ludvig Olson's 1916 dissertation, submitted to the University of Chicago for a doctorate in English, studies the relation of Hrolfs Saga Kraka and the Bjarkarimur to Beowulf. It is a contribution to the history of saga development in England and the Scandinavian countries.

Bibliography and abbreviations open the work, with line numbers following A. J. Wyatt's edition of Beowulf and references to journals of Nordic philology and history. Olson traces shared heroes, plots and motifs across Old English and Old Norse texts. The private edition, distributed by Chicago libraries, remains a scholarly source for readers tracing Beowulf's northern kin.
15148-six-feet-four:
Jackson Gregory's 1917 Western opens in a mountain storm that snaps tall pines and darkens the canyons by midday. Chapters follow Buck Thornton, a man's man, through a ford, a ranch on Big Little River, and a dance at Deer Creek schoolhouse. Rattlesnake Pollard, the Bedloe boys, and a frame-up raise the stakes.

Winifred judges a man, Jimmie squares himself, and a showdown looms as a gentleman from New Mexico enters the game. Gregory writes in the pulp Western style, with action, romance, and frontier justice. Fans of classic Westerns will enjoy the storm, the ranch feuds, and the tall hero of the title.
15563-reason-and-faith-their-claims-and-:
Henry Rogers wrote this review essay for the Edinburgh Review of October 1849, pages 293 to 356, on reason and faith, their claims and conflicts. It reviews three books: Whately's Historic Doubts on Napoleon, Froude's Nemesis of Faith, and Foxton's Popular Christianity. The essay opens with an old divine's image: reason and faith as the patriarch's two sons, reason firstborn, faith inheriting the blessing.

Rogers calls that image ingenious but unjust. Human beings trust and believe long before they reason or know, he argues, and both powers are coeval with human nature, meant to dwell together and complete each other. The essay then tests rationalist readings of scripture, asking on what ground parts of a record can be rejected as improbable. It is a learned Victorian defense of faith that still reasons, not a plea for blind belief.
1822-the-amateur:
Richard Harding Davis sets this sea story in February off the Banks, where the weather is so thick that on the upper decks one could have driven a sleigh. Inside the smoking-room, Austin Ford shelters from the blizzard. He listens to talk of Harry, a fellow passenger who is at meals three times a day and on deck all the rest of the day.

The amateur of the title is a man out of his depth. The story turns on what happens when a landsman tries the sea's work. Davis, who knew ships and sailors, writes the cold, the fog, and the talk of the smoking-room with care. The tale's tension comes from a simple question: can a gentleman passenger become a seaman when it matters.
1976-peter-ruff-and-the-double-four:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's Peter Ruff and the Double Four introduces Mr. Peter Ruff. He leaves a respectable life to become a private agent for those who cannot go to the police. The contents run from Introducing Mr. Peter Ruff through Vincent Cawdor, commission agent, to Delilah from Streatham and the little lady from the country.

A scene in which a woman protests that Count von Hern has not been found, and that she saw him dancing with a tall girl in yellow, shows Oppenheim's method. The method uses a ballroom, a secret, and a hero who sees what others miss. The book gathers Ruff's cases into a single volume, and it remains a polished sample of the Edwardian adventure story.
19951-ted-strong-in-montana-or-with-lari:
Edward C. Taylor wrote the Ted Strong books, boys' westerns under the Rough Rider banner. Ted Strong in Montana opens with hard luck on the trail. High water at Poplar Fork has delayed the outfit a week. Had they left earlier, Ted says, they'd be settled at the ranch for winter. Lariat and spur, the subtitle promises, will settle things instead. Snow and rivers set the terms in Montana.

Ted Strong led his Rough Riders through many volumes of adventure. Taylor's West is work first: cattle, weather, and distance. Boys learned ranch craft between the stampedes. Montana gives this volume big country and hard winters. The series rivaled the era's other western franchises. It shows the boys' western at full gallop.
20534-a-sermon-preached-at-the-quaker-s-:
Preached at the Quakers' meeting house in Gracechurch Street, London, this sermon addresses a painful split inside the Society of Friends. The preacher speaks while proceedings in the Society are stirring strong feeling. He knows his words will be read as taking a side.

He states most plainly that the publication is no party act. It does not spring from party feeling, he says, though he must take a heartfelt interest in the matter. He feels deeply that even a friend of the cause must speak with care. The sermon preserves one voice from a forgotten Quaker quarrel.
2097-the-sign-of-the-four:
Arthur Conan Doyle's second Sherlock Holmes novel opens with Holmes at his syringe, then plunges into the case of Mary Morstan and a treasure from India. A bald-headed man, a tragedy at Pondicherry Lodge, and the Baker Street Irregulars follow. Doyle wrote The Sign of the Four in 1890, as the second Holmes novel after A Study in Scarlet.

Holmes and Watson track Jonathan Small and the Agra treasure down the Thames, and Small's strange story explains the crime. The book sets the Holmes pattern: deduction, chase, and a long confession that ties the threads together. The Agra treasure links London crime to Indian mutiny history, a link Doyle uses with care.
22259-the-legacy-of-greece-essays-by-gil:
Gilbert Murray edited The Legacy of Greece in 1921, gathering essays by leading British scholars. Murray himself, Oxford's professor of Greek, opens the volume with a challenge. If man's life were measured in dollars, miles, and horse-power, he writes, Greece must count as a poverty-stricken minute territory. Its engines stood nearer the spear and bow than the telegraph and aeroplane.

Yet Greece, the essays argue, founded Europe's reason, art, politics, and science. W. R. Inge writes on religion, J. Burnet on philosophy, and others on literature, art, and thought. The Legacy series shaped how Britain taught its civilisational debts. This first volume is its confident manifesto for the classics.
23091-the-troubadour:
Peter Michael Sherman packs a party with talk in The Troubadour. The narrator's attention wanders from the Kutrov-Alva variations, since Bill has been speaking for ten minutes and cannot be expected to arrive at any point for at least another fifteen. From the east come apocalyptic figures of nuclear physics. From the west, Mondrian interwoven with Picasso. From the south side of the room comes a dissection of the newest betrayal of popular hopes. Northward, the mysteries of atonality.

That compass of chatter maps a whole intellectual generation at one gathering. Sherman's troubadour sings among people who argue art, politics, and physics as party games. The piece belongs to the little-magazine world of clever talk. Its pleasure is eavesdropping, catching a vanished salon mid-buzz, ideologies and all.
2789-the-motor-girls-on-a-tour:
Margaret Penrose wrote this Motor Girls adventure, following the success of the Motor Boys series by Clarence Young. Readers had asked for a similar series for girls, and Penrose, author of the Dorothy Dale books, was chosen to furnish these tales.

The Motor Girls tour by car, with mishaps, mysteries, and friendships along the road. Penrose writes in the brisk series style, with plucky heroines and clean fun. The book delights as an early girls' motoring adventure, from an age when a car tour was still a daring feat. The road gives the girls freedom their mothers never knew.
2922-the-past-condition-of-organic-natur:
Thomas Henry Huxley delivered this lecture to working men at the Museum of Practical Geology in 1863, as the second of six on Darwin's Origin of Species. Huxley first sketches the present condition of organic nature, summing up the multiplicity of animal forms and the broad principles visible to an attentive eye. He then turns backward, asking what the rocks and fossils say about earlier life.

The lecture warns against easy readings of the strata, noting that one layer may have been laid down ages before another despite appearances. Huxley cites Sir Henry De la Beche on that fallacy and works through figures to make the point. The talk remains a clear example of Victorian science teaching, plain in language and careful in argument.
3694-every-man-in-his-humour:
Ben Jonson, the rival and friend of Shakespeare, wrote this comedy of London life around the old notion of humours, the idea that each person is ruled by one ruling bent. A jealous merchant, a fretful father, and a swaggering soldier cross paths with a crew of young gallants in shops, streets, and homes. Each acts out his fixed folly while others scheme to profit from it. The play mixes sharp talk with slapstick, and its jokes land through character rather than plot twists.

Jonson first staged the piece in 1598, and it helped make his name as a comic writer. The long opening essay in this edition sketches his hard youth, his schooling under William Camden, and his rise among the players. Readers new to Jonson get a lively way into his world, where vanity, greed, and love all wear the same city clothes and trip over each other.
3695-every-man-out-of-his-humour:
Ben Jonson writes a comedy of humours, performed in 1599 as a companion to his earlier Every Man in His Humour. The play's characters are out of their humour, meaning out of balance, and Jonson satirizes courtiers, poets, soldiers, and gallants who mistake fashion for nature. An introduction sketches Jonson himself, a large man who as a youth enlisted as a soldier, trailing his pike in Flanders in the wars of William the Silent against Spain.

Jonson later became a literary dictator and poet laureate, shaping English letters more than any man of his time. His comedy mixes sharp verse with stage business and direct address to the audience. The play suits readers interested in Elizabethan theater and in Jonson's bold, combative art.
6172-god-and-my-neighbour:
Robert Blatchford, calling himself Nunquam, dedicates God and My Neighbour to his son Robert Corri Blatchford. His preface takes up the word infidel in capitals, a new name bestowed by Christian gentlemen as reproach, though to his ears it sounds quaint and not unpleasing.

The notorious infidel editor of the Clarion, one true believer calls him, and the words return to Blatchford on a walk along the pleasant Strand with his favorite black pipe. He asks which is worse, demagogue or infidel, and answers he is both. Blatchford writes freethought with humor, pipe smoke, and plain challenge.
6582-in-the-court-of-king-arthur:
Samuel Lowe writes a boys' Arthur tale around a lad named Allan, who finds a champion, goes forth, and meets the knights of the Round Table. Combats, a tournament, Merlin's message, and the prowess of Tristram fill the early chapters, while later ones send Allan toward King Mark's foul plan and a rescue. A kitchen boy, a stranger, and Sir Launcelot all cross his path.

The tale moves from Camelot to Normandy and back, with Gareth, Galahad, and a beggar tied to the Grail quest. Lowe keeps the story clear and the deeds bold, so young readers can follow the code of knighthood. In the Court of King Arthur is a plain, stirring retelling of old legend for a new young audience.
7425-the-louisa-alcott-reader-a-suppleme:
Louisa M. Alcott's stories were a staple of American schoolrooms, and this reader gathers them for the fourth year of school. Its contents run from A Christmas Dream and The Candy Country to Naughty Jocko, The Skipping Shoes, and Rosy's Journey. How They Ran Away, The Fairy Box, and The Piggy Girl complete a set chosen for young readers.

The opening story sets the pattern: a discontented girl, tired of Christmas and its same old surprises, learns what the holiday can still mean. Alcott's tales mix fantasy with home lessons, always in plain, warm language a child can read aloud. As a school reader, the book was meant to teach reading through delight, and it still works that way.
794-the-wouldbegoods-being-the-further-a:
E. Nesbit brought back the Bastable children in this sequel to The Treasure Seekers, now bent on being good. Their would-be good deeds go gloriously wrong, from jungle games to a tower of mystery, a circus, and a high-born babe in need of care. Each chapter turns a kind plan into comic chaos.

Oswald and his siblings mean well, and their blunders teach them patience and sense. Nesbit's voice is warm, funny, and true to childhood, and the tales have delighted readers for generations. The book stands with its predecessor as a classic of family adventure, where goodness is learned by trial and error.
8193-the-sceptics-of-the-old-testament-j:
E. J. Dillon, late professor of comparative philology at Kharkoff and doctor of oriental languages at Louvain, presented Job, Koheleth, and Agur as the sceptics of the Old Testament. With English text translated for the first time from the primitive Hebrew as restored on recent philological discoveries. Dedicated to Alexander Vassilyevitch Paschkoff, the volume argues that these three books voice doubt and questioning within Scripture itself.

Dillon's restoration claims to recover an earlier Hebrew text, and his translations aim to let Job's protests, Ecclesiastes' vanity, and Agur's riddles speak freshly. Scholars debate his reconstructions, but the book's thesis endures: the Bible contains its own sceptics. For biblical students, it is a bold, learned attempt to hear doubt as part of faith.
8497-the-poems-and-prose-of-ernest-dowso:
Arthur Symons wrote the memoir that opens this collection of Ernest Dowson's poems and prose, and the contents that follow show why Dowson mattered. Poems include Nuns of the Perpetual Adoration, Villanelle of Sunset, and To One in Bedlam. Amor Umbratilis and Non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae follow, the famous lament for Cynara, with prose pieces after.

Dowson, a poet of the decadent nineties, died young, and Symons's memoir frames his brief, troubled life. Readers meet the lyric voice of the Yellow Book era: musical, melancholy, and haunted by lost love. The volume remains the standard introduction to Dowson, through a friend who knew him well.
9098-tacitus-and-bracciolini-the-annals-:
John Wilson Ross wrote this bold attack on a classic text, first published without his name in 1878. He argues that the Annals of Tacitus, the Roman historian, were forged in the fifteenth century by Poggio Bracciolini, a humanist famed for finding old manuscripts. Ross calls the case a question against all received tradition.

Latin quotes from scholars of the day back his charge, and he stresses Bracciolini's skill at imitation. Most scholars reject the claim today, yet the book fascinates. It shows how far doubt about ancient texts can run, and why proof matters in history.
9470-his-hour:
Elinor Glyn, famed for Three Weeks, wrote His Hour in 1910, a romance of Russian high society. The book is called When the Hour Came in England and Russia. Glyn dedicated it to the Grand Duchess Vladimir, who aided her study of Russian character and heard the tale read aloud. A prince named Milaslavski stands at the heart of the story, seen first at a fancy ball in the Winter Palace.

The novel moves through balls, palaces, and proud hearts, as love tests rank and duty in imperial Russia. Glyn writes with lush, frank feeling, and a keen eye for dress, manners, and power. A reader gets a vivid, old-style romance of a vanished court, told by a writer who knew its rooms first hand.
952-tom-swift-and-his-air-glider-or-seek:
A breakdown and a daring project start this Tom Swift tale by Victor Appleton, in which Tom seeks a platinum treasure in Russia. The hand of the Czar, a clue from Russia, and the rescue of Mr. Petrofsky lead to the building of an air glider, a craft that can ride the winds where engines fail.

In a great gale and a storm at sea, spies dog the party, and the airship carries them toward the treasure. Appleton mixes Russian intrigue with aeronautical daring, and Tom's cool head saves the day. The book is a brisk Tom Swift adventure, where a glider, not a gun, wins the prize.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assur:
Assur carries three meanings in this entry. First, it is the Old Testament name for the Assyrian land and nation. Second, it names one of Shem's sons in Genesis 10:22. In verse 11 the Douay version's Out of that land came forth Assur should read differently in the original. There Nimrod went forth into Assyria, since the name there means country, not person. Another Assur, or Ashur, father of Tekoa, appears in Chronicles.

Third, Assur is the national god of Assyrians, in cuneiform Asshur or Ashur. Assyrian religion, like its language and arts, derived in all essentials from Babylonians, but as Assyrian power rose over southern provinces, its local tutelary deity rose with it. Asshur, first the eponymous god of Assyria's capital, also called Asshur, thus grew into a national god. The entry separates land, person, and deity sharing one name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chur:
The Diocese of Chur, ancient Curia Rhaetorum, covers the Swiss cantons of Graubünden, Glarus, Zürich, Unterwalden, and Uri, with the little principality of Liechtenstein. Chur itself, the bishop's seat and capital of Graubünden, was once a Roman fortified camp and now holds about 10,000 people, a third of them Catholic. A Bishop of Chur, Saint Asimo, appears as early as the 451 Synod of Milan.

Local tradition names Saint Lucius, a reputed king of Britain martyred about 176, as the first bishop and chief patron, and his relics rest in the cathedral. The see passed from Milan to Mainz after Verdun in 843, then directly to the Holy See in 1803. Arian pressure under Goths and Lombards, quarrels of emperor and pope, and the Reformation, proclaimed at Chur in 1524, all scarred the diocese. Its ninety-sixth bishop, John Fidelis Battaglia, was consecrated in March 1889.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
The Clerks Regular of Our Saviour took present form at Benoite-Vaux in 1851, in the Verdun diocese. They carry the constitutions and spirit of the Canons Regular of Our Saviour. Saint Peter Fourier, canon of Chamousay, founded those canons as a Lorraine reform in 1623, confirmed by Urban the Eighth in 1628. Their scope, in Fourier's summary, was Christian education of youth and sacred ministry among the poor and neglected. Across Lorraine and into France and Savoy the order flourished, but the Revolution destroyed it.

In 1851 four zealous priests of Verdun withdrew to the shrine of Our Lady of Benoite-Vaux to revive Fourier's labours. There they began religious life by Fourier's rule for his canons. Three years later the Holy See approved them, changing their name from Canons Regular to Clerks Regular. Over the next half century the congregation spread to several houses for the education of youth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-day-of-atonem:
A liturgical entry explains the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, the most solemn fast of the Jewish year, kept on the tenth day of Tishri, in September or October. Leviticus chapter 16 sets out its rites: no food all day, no servile work, and sacrifices of a calf, a ram, and seven lambs.

Its distinctive ceremony used two goats. Lots chose one for the Lord, offered for sin, and one as the emissary goat, sent alive into the wilderness. Aaron laid both hands on the living goat, confessed Israel's iniquities upon its head, and sent it away bearing sins into an uninhabited land. The entry notes how Jewish prayers for the day foreshadow Christian liturgies' commemoration of saints and the faithful departed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exequatur:
Exequatur is a faculty by which civil rulers give a papal Bull or Brief binding force in their lands. The ruler first examines the law and finds it does not harm civil rights. Modern statesmen split it from the Regium Placet. The Placet covers acts of home church superiors, while the Exequatur covers papal acts from a foreign power.

No trace of such a state right appears in the early centuries, or even in the fourteenth. It grew from care during the Western Schism, when Urban VI let superiors test papal letters for forgery. Martin V condemned the Placet in 1418, but Portugal, Naples, France, and Spain revived it. Luther, Gallicans, and Jansenists defended it, but the article calls it false in law, since the Church holds power straight from her Founder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-eust:
Francois Eustache Lesueur was a Jesuit missionary and student of language at the Abnaki mission in Canada, whose very name and dates are uncertain. The entry traces the confusion to the English burning of the St. Francis mission and its records in 1759. Born near Coutances in Normandy on 22 July 1685 or 1686, though Maurault gives Lunel in Languedoc, he died at Montreal on 28 or 26 April 1760. Maurault's account puts his death at Quebec in 1755. He is variously called Francois Eustache, Jacques Francois, or simply Jacques.

 Besides prayers and sermons in Abnaki, he wrote a valuable account of the famed Calumet Dance, a ceremonial dance of welcome and alliance. It preserves a Native ritual that missionaries otherwise recorded only in passing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-vava:
Francois Vavasseur, born at Paray-le-Monial on 8 December 1605 and dead at Paris on 16 December 1681, was a Jesuit humanist and controversialist. He entered the Society on 25 October 1621, taught humanities and rhetoric for seven years, then positive theology and Scripture at Bourges and later Paris. His first work paraphrased Job in Latin hexameters in 1637, resumed with commentary in 1679, and he published the Theurgicon on Christ's miracles in 1644 and a book of elegies in 1656.

He took an active part in the Jansenist controversy with Cornelius Jansenius Iprensis suspectus in 1650 and defended himself against a charge of writing pamphlets on the Calaghan affair in 1653. There he defined the Port-Royal style before the Provinciales as monotonous, colourless, and burdened with involved periods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hector-st-joh:
French farmer Hector St. John de Crèvecoeur, born at Caen in 1731, emigrated to America in 1754 and became the voice of the American cultivator for French readers. Arrested by the English as a suspected spy on a return to France in 1780, he spent months in confinement, then interested Normandy farmers in growing the potato during a three-year stay.

Back in America, his praise of the land's richness drew several hundred countrymen to a Pennsylvania colony, later destroyed with its settlers massacred. After the Revolution he served long as French consul at New York, helped found St. Peter's, the city's first Catholic church, and wrote Letters of an American Farmer in 1784 and a Voyage through upper Pennsylvania and New York in 1801, both admired for their style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-honour:
Honour is the deferential recognition, by word or sign, of another person's worth or station. A person shows it by giving another his title, raising his hat, or yielding a place of precedence. Such acts express a sense of the other's worth and, at the same time, profess one's own lower place.

Marks of honour suit worth of any kind, unless some special reason bars them, and people owe honour to all who stand above them. First comes God, worshipped as first beginning and last end. Then angels and saints for God's gifts to them, and parents for life and upbringing. Rulers spiritual and temporal earn honour for God-given authority, the aged for presumed wisdom, and moral worth and great talent wherever they appear.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-institute-of-:
Julie Billiart and Marie-Louise-Françoise Blin de Bourdon, Countess of Gézaincourt, founded this teaching congregation at Amiens in 1803. Father Joseph Varin, discerning Julie's fitness for the task, ordered her in God's name to form a congregation for the education of youth, and a patron paid the first costs. On 5 August 1803 the foundresses took a house in Rue Neuve with eight orphans entrusted to them.

In the house chapel on 2 February 1803, the two foundresses and their postulant Catherine Duchatel vowed chastity. They added a vow to give themselves to the Christian schooling of girls. They also vowed to train religious teachers to go wherever they were asked. From that cradle house the institute grew into a teaching order. Readers get the founding story in close, dated detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-arthur:
Dominican friar James Arthur, also called Didacus Arturus, was a noted theologian born at Limerick early in the seventeenth century. He probably died in 1670. He joined the Dominicans at St Stephen's convent, Salamanca, Spain. He taught theology in various houses of his order, especially at Salamanca, with great credit and profit to his students. In 1640 he was called to Coimbra university as first professor of theology.

He held that chair until 1642, when Portugal separated from Spain. He was expelled for refusing an oath to defend the Immaculate Conception doctrine. He returned to St Dominic's convent in Lisbon. There he lived for many years preparing a commentary on Aquinas' Summa. The planned work was to run to ten volumes. His death prevented its completion. The entry presents a scholar whose oath refusal cost him a chair.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Meilleur, a French-Canadian physician and educator born in 1796 and dead in 1878, built Lower Canada's public schools. He studied classics at Montreal's Sulpician college, philosophy in New Hampshire, and medicine in Vermont, and helped found the college of L'Assomption.

Meilleur sat in parliament in 1834 and served as the province's first superintendent of education from 1842 to 1855. He enforced the union education law against prejudice and party pressure, organised the department, and saw primary and classical schooling grow with clergy support. His textbooks and his 1860 Memorial of Education record a life spent making schooling a public good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois:
Jean-François Lesueur, a French composer born near Abbeville in 1760 and dead in Paris in 1837, became a chorister at seven and studied at Amiens. He served as music master at Séez, Dijon, Le Mans, Tours, and the Holy Innocents in Paris, winning Notre-Dame's directorship in 1786.

Lesueur aimed to stir devotion through imagination, even prefacing a Mass with an operatic overture, a move that stirred the musical world. Attacked anonymously in 1787, he answered with a pamphlet on music fitted to each feast. When Notre-Dame cut his orchestra for cost, he resigned in 1788 and withdrew to a friend's country house for four years of fresh work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-barbour:
John Barbour was a Scottish churchman and the earliest poet and first detailed historian of Scotland. Born about 1320, he was already Archdeacon of Aberdeen in 1357. He traveled to Oxford and France on royal passports for study, served as a commissioner for the ransom of David II, and audited the exchequer. Royal pensions rewarded his patriotic poem, including twenty shillings a year which he left to fund Masses for himself and his parents.

Writing in the northern dialect of Middle English later called Scots, Barbour composed The Bruce. It is a long narrative poem begun in 1375 on Robert the Bruce and the wars of independence, surviving in manuscripts of 1487 and 1489. Lost works included The Brut and a history of the Stewarts. The entry sets out the documents of his life, his offices and income, and the place of his poem at the head of Scottish literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-winte:
John of Winterthur was a Swiss Franciscan chronicler whose history illuminates the first half of the fourteenth century. Born about 1300 at Winterthur, he attended his town school from 1309 to 1315. He lived as a Franciscan at Basle in 1328, Villingen in 1336, and Lindau from 1343, dying after 1348, probably at Zurich.

Begun in 1340, his chronicle from Emperor Frederick II to 1348 is a full history to that year, with annals thereafter. It remains a fruitful source on the age. It gives a clear picture of the conflicts between Swabia's cities and nobles and a general view of imperial events. It covers especially how Louis the Bavarian dealt with the papacy and the Franciscan Order's stance in that quarrel, which John championed ardently. A man of culture in sacred and secular letters, he was also credulous, delighting in others' observations. That fault makes his work valuable for the history of civilization.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-gaston-:
Louis Gaston de Segur was a French prelate and apologist, born at Paris in 1820 and dead there in 1881. Descended from a marshal of France on his father's side, and from Rostopchin, who burned Moscow in 1812, on his mother's, he turned from diplomacy and painting to the priesthood. He was ordained in 1847.

He served Paris children, the poor, and imprisoned soldiers, then spent four years at Rome as auditor of the Rota, esteemed by Pius IX. Blindness forced his return in 1856, with episcopal honours but no see. He then poured time, preaching, and money into apprentices' patronage and workingmen's unions. Seminaries, army chaplaincies, and the evangelization of Paris suburbs also drew his care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-pasteur:
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and founder of bacteriology, born at Dole in 1822 and dead near Sevres in 1895. Son of a poor tanner at Arbois, he first dreamed of painting, then caught fire for science at Besancon and under Dumas, Balard, and Biot at Paris.

His first triumph untangled tartaric acid crystals, showing that look-alike crystals differed in how they turned polarized light. That led him to dissymmetry, the twist found in living products but not in minerals. Later work on fermentation, disease, and vaccines made his name world-famous, and the Pasteur Institute, opened in 1889, crowned a career that joined pure science to medicine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-dominiq:
Auguste Sibour was Archbishop of Paris, born at Saint-Paul-Trois-Chateaux in 1792 and dead at Paris in 1857. In 1837 he ran Nimes as administrator during a vacancy, and in 1839 became Bishop of Digne.

At Digne he fostered church studies, raised his chapter's role, and kept canonical forms strictly in church trials. The same temper marked his Paris rule, to which he rose largely for prompt support of the new government after the 1848 Revolution. In 1853 he married Napoleon III, who had made him senator the year before. He called the Immaculate Conception definition inopportune in his reply to Pius IX, yet attended its promulgation and published it in his diocese. Imperial help let him aid poor churches and found new parishes, and he pushed the Roman Rite in Paris until an interdicted priest named Verger murdered him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mathias-hauze:
Mathias Hauzeur was a Franciscan theologian, born at Verviers in 1589 and dead at Liege in 1676, who long taught in schools. He wrote twenty works and won fame debating Calvinist preacher Gabriel Hotton from 19 to 22 April 1633. He pressed it so successfully that nearby Catholics lit bonfires to celebrate his triumph.

He told that tale in Accusation et conviction du Sieur Hotton of 1633, also put out in Latin. Other works include Catholic Exorcisms of 1634 against Hotton and Equulcus ecclesiasticus of 1635 against Samuel des Maretz. His Praejudicia augustissima of 1634 set out Augustine for the true Church, with a French synopsis. His chief works are his Anatomia of Augustine's doctrine of 1643 to 1645 and his Collatio Totius Theologiae of 1652, a gloss on the Sentences' later books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monseigneur:
Monseigneur is a French honorific built from words for my and lord. It matches English my lord and Italian monsignore. While monsieur spread to every man of good society, Monseigneur kept its ceremonial weight. In church usage it is reserved for bishops and archbishops. It is used before the name, as in Monseigneur Dupanloup.

The entry notes its finer points. It was once placed before the name alone rather than the title. Modern use gives the form for a bishop by title. Confusion can arise with the Italian Monsignore, a title for Roman prelates. In Italy bishops instead bear Excellency. In France only the Archbishop of Reims, as born legate, holds that style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nagpur:
Nagpur is a diocese in India, suffragan to Madras, formerly the northwestern part of the Vicariate Apostolic of Vizagapatam. It was erected as a diocese on 29 July 1887, with boundaries finally readjusted on 10 July 1895. It covers most of the Central Provinces, Berar, part of Indore State, and a strip of the Nizam's dominions to the Godavery River, spanning about 124,000 square miles.

Its Catholic population numbers 15,000 among about 15,000,000 people, served by 28 Missionaries of Saint Francis de Sales and 7 secular clergy, with brothers, sisters and catechists assisting. The diocese holds 12 churches and 33 chapels, with cathedral, bishop's residence and seminary at Nagpur. No missionary is traced there before the nineteenth century, when Goan priests first visited Nagpur, Kamptee, Aurangabad and Jaulnah.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-namur:
Namur is a Belgian diocese constituted by the bull of 12 May 1559 from territory of Liege, made suffragan of the new metropolitan see of Cambrai. The Concordat of 1801 re-established it to match the Department of Sambre-et-Meuse, suffragan of Mechlin. In 1823 it gained Luxemburg from Metz, and after the 1830 revolution its jurisdiction settled in 1842 to the two Belgian provinces of Namur and Luxemburg.

In 1047 Albert II, Count of Namur, raised a collegiate church on an ancient chapel site, served by twelve canons with rights of justice in their lands. Its first dean was Frederick of Lorraine. The entry follows the diocese through its bishops, chapters, parishes and schools, its shrines and religious orders. It traces the church's life in a province long contested between France, Spain, Austria and the Netherlands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-du-boi:
Pierre du Bois, Baron d'Avaugour, was Canada's sixth governor-general, dying in 1664. Born of an ancient Breton family, he served forty years in the French army, travelled Persia, Russia, Poland, and Sweden, and fought all Germany's campaigns. Chosen in 1661 to succeed d'Argenson, he reached Quebec on 31 August, set out at once for Montreal to learn the country's state.

He advised fortifying Quebec, replacing useless officials with soldiers to check the Iroquois and stop Dutch arms supplies. He formed a council headed by the Jesuit superior and banned liquor sales to Indians under pain of death. Quarrelling with bishop and Jesuits over a widow jailed for selling brandy, he dissolved his council and lifted the ban, and disorders followed. Relieved of command, he left Quebec on 23 July 1663, advised driving the Dutch from Fort Orange, then died defending Zrin against the Turks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rocamadour:
Rocamadour is a French pilgrimage village in Quercy whose sanctuary of the Virgin has drawn kings, bishops, and nobles for centuries. The town stands in the Lot, in the diocese of Cahors. Its name is traditionally traced to St Amadour. Legend identifies him with Zacchaeus of the Gospel, husband of Veronica. With her he sailed from Palestine to Aquitaine, met St Martial, visited Rome, and retired to a wild spot where he built a chapel to the Virgin.

That marvellous account appears only long after its supposed age. Amadour's name occurs in no document before his Acts, no older than the twelfth century. St Martial lived in the third century, not the first. The Acts are therefore judged a forgery. Guesses identifying Amadour with an unknown hermit or St Amator of Auxerre are mere hypothesis. The sanctuary's true origin is lost in antiquity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-flour:
Saint-Flour is the diocese covering the department of Cantal in France, under the archbishop of Bourges, and it was re-established by the Concordat of 1802. Haute-Loire, first joined to it, was detached in 1823 when the see of Le Puy was restored. Its namesake, Saint Florus, is said to have been the first bishop of Lodève. He is said to have died at Indiciat while preaching in Haute-Auvergne, though one scholar places him in the fifth century at the Council of Arles.

A monastery already stood at Indiciat late in the tenth century, passed to Odilo of Cluny, was seized and wrecked, then restored between 1025 and 1031. Urban II consecrated its new church after the Council of Clermont in 1095, and the church later collapsed in 1396. John XXII raised Saint-Flour to a bishopric in August 1317.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-thomas-:
Saint Thomas of Mylapur names a diocese in India, suffragan of Goa, whose cathedral stands where tradition buries the apostle Thomas. Mylapur means town of peacocks in Tamil, rendered Meliapor by the Portuguese and Mylapore by the English. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with the Indian tradition that Thomas preached on both coasts of India.

Hostility from pagan priests, the story runs, drove him to St Thomas's Mount four miles south-west. There his persecutors ran him through with a lance as he knelt in prayer in the year 68. The entry then follows the see through Portuguese and later history, weighing local tradition against outside evidence. Readers get both the apostle's legend and the growth of a living Indian diocese around his shrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-william:
Simon William Gabriel Bruté de Rémur, first Bishop of Vincennes, Indiana, was born at Rennes, France, on 20 March 1779 and died at Vincennes on 26 June 1839. His father superintended the royal domains in Brittany. Young Bruté's schooling was broken by the Revolution, and he learned the compositor's trade in his widowed mother's printing house. He visited prisons and carried letters and the Blessed Sacrament to jailed clergy.

He studied medicine, graduating in 1803, but turned at once to church studies, later teaching at Mount Saint Mary's under the Sulpicians. In 1834 he was named to the new See of Vincennes, covering all Indiana and eastern Illinois. Consecrated at Saint Louis that October, he traveled his vast diocese, then raised priests and funds in France for churches and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sophie-rostop:
Sophie Rostopchine, Comtesse de Segur, was a Russian-born French author of children's stories. This brief entry sketches a life lived between two empires. Born in 1797, she was the daughter of General Rostopchine. He ordered Moscow burned after Borodino in 1812, and so forced Napoleon into his disastrous retreat.

Married to Eugene, Comte de Segur, she became a woman of culture and uncommon literary talent. She wrote stories for the Bibliotheque Rose, a series of short novels for young readers. Among them were Pauvre Blaise, Le General Dourakine, Un bon petit diable, and Les vacances. Those books made her name familiar to generations of French children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-arthur:
Thomas Arthur, a celebrated Irish physician of the seventeenth century, was born at Limerick in 1593 and died about 1666. Little survives about him beyond his own Latin writings: a genealogical account in verse and a diary of his cases, both kept in the British Museum. Educated at Bordeaux, he studied medicine in Paris and began practice in Limerick in 1619.

Success carried him to Dublin in 1624, and a cure of Archbishop Ussher at Drogheda made his name among the English, earning him fifty-one pounds. His diary records fees, patients and cures in detail, and shows a doctor held in high regard. He sometimes styled himself Thomas Arthur FitzWilliam, after his father William.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-vavaso:
Thomas Vavasour, an English Catholic physician born about 1536, spent his last years in prison for his faith, dying at Hull in May 1585. A pensioner of St. John's College, Cambridge, he disputed for transubstantiation and the sacrifice of the Mass before the king's commissioners in 1549. He then took a medical degree at Venice and a licence to practise from the London College of Physicians in 1556.

At his York house Mass was said in 1570, and in 1572 he was accused of sheltering Edmund Campion. Confined to his house for nine months, he was sent to solitary confinement in Hull Castle in November 1574. Archbishop Grindal called him sophistical and disdainful in argument. Released after submitting on the royal supremacy, he was jailed again as a recusant and died in Hull Castle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trichur:
A church district in India, one of three vicariates for Christians of the Syrian rite. It lies between Mangalore in the north, Coimbatore in the east, Ernaculam in the south and the sea in the west.

The census of 1900 counted 91,998 Catholics of the Syrian rite, with 63 churches and 23 chapels served by 66 local priests. Three houses of Carmelite monks and four convents of Carmelite nuns serve the district, and its schools number 2 high schools, 2 lower schools and 184 small schools teaching 19,093 children. John Menacherry, made vicar in 1896, lives at Trichur, and a school for priests there sends men on to Puthenpally or Kandy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-st:
William of Saint-Amour was a thirteenth-century Paris theologian who led the secular masters against the mendicant friars. Born in Burgundy in the early 1200s, he died at Paris about 1273. About 1250 he became a theology teacher at Paris, and a few years later headed the seculars in their quarrel with the Dominicans and Franciscans over university rights and preaching.

In 1256 he issued De Periculis Novissimorum Temporum, attacking mendicancy itself as unchristian and closer to Antichrist than to Christ, mocking friars' ways with merciless wit. Alexander IV at Anagni condemned the tract to burning and banished William from France that same year. A second blast, the Book of Antichrist, followed ten years later. William returned to Paris in 1263 and taught again, though his tract later hindered more than helped the university cause.
doe-osti-2588972-investigating-the-impac: Surface impurities got their impact study, and this DOE report investigates absorbed CO, CO2, CH4, and H2. The pages detail the findings. The materials scientists get their data. The impurities were absorbed surface. The gases were CO and CO2. The scientists got data.
doe-osti-2997328-understanding-geometry-: LPBF geometry got linked to microstructure, and this DOE report connects lab studies to real parts. The pages detail the case studies. The additive folks get their insight. The process was LPBF. The studies were lab scale. The folks were additive.
doe-osti-2998274-wave-optics-simulation-: Fourier holography got its wave-optics framework, and this DOE report covers XMCD simulations. The pages detail the transform work. The x-ray folks get their toolkit. The holography was Fourier transform. The work was transform. The folks were x-ray.
doe-osti-3014718-bio-derived-hydrogen-pe: Hydrogen peroxide got bio-derived, and this DOE CRADA final makes it from paper waste. The pages detail the manufacturing findings. The chemists get their closeout. The waste was pulp and paper. The closeout was chemist. The peroxide was hydrogen.
doe-osti-3018515-biomolecular-films-for-: Biomolecular films got DAC-tasked, and this DOE text captures CO2 from air. The pages detail the findings. The climate folks get their data. The films were biomolecular. The data were climate. The CO2 was capture. The air was direct.
doe-osti-3364334-enhanced-component-perf: Turbine pumps got performance-studied, and this DOE text covers 1998-2024. The pages detail the enhanced findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The study was component. The data were nuclear. The 1998-2024 were turbine. The driven were turbine. The pumps were study.
doe-osti-3375571-assessing-options-for-p: Wood heaters got particulate-assessed, and this DOE CRADA final covers tools. The pages detail the options findings. The energy folks get their closeout. The report was final. The closeout was energy. The heaters were wood. The tools were options.
doe-osti-3602536-orbiting-carbon-observa: OCO-2 got Lamont-validated, and this DOE interim covers spectrometer validation. The pages detail the orbiting findings. The climate folks get their data. The campaign was field. The data were climate. The Oklahoma were Lamont. The spectrometer were validation. The transform were Fourier.
every-man-in-his-humour:
Ben Jonson won his first stage fame with Every Man in His Humour, and the hosted text keeps the early Florence setting. Lorenzo di Pazzi, a merchant, frets that his son wastes his gifts on poetry. Servant Musco schemes, quick with disguises and plots. Jonson builds the comedy on humours, the idea that one trait rules each person's conduct.

Young Lorenzo loves verse more than business, to his father's disgust. Cousin Stephano, a country fool, buys a hawk and begs a book to learn hawking from print. Braggart Bobadill boasts of battles he never fought, in the play's most quoted talk. Jealousy, gulling, and errands tangle the young men of Florence into knots. A wise judge figure untangles the mess and sends each fool home exposed. Drama readers use the play to watch Jonson invent English comedy of humours, the form that shaped city comedy for a century.
every-man-out-of-his-humour:
Ben Jonson, Shakespeare's rival, built Every Man Out of His Humour as a comedy of humours, the theory that one fluid rules each temper. Envious Macilente opens the play, sick with spite at every man's good fortune. Two chorus figures, Cordatus and Mitis, pause the action to defend the author's design. Jonson meant the stage to purge folly by laughing at it.

Fops, braggarts, and social climbers parade through the scenes, each ruled by one passion. Sogliardo, a rich clown, buys gentility he cannot wear with grace. Carlo Buffone spews abuse at everyone, while Fastidious Brisk apes court manners and dress. Deliro dotes on a wife whose brother sees the folly plainly. One by one, events knock each figure out of his humour, curing obsession by exposure. Readers of drama find Jonson at his most systematic here: a London of types, sorted, mocked, and dosed with their medicine.
god-and-my-neighbour:
God and My Neighbour, by Robert Blatchford, is the freethought testament of the socialist editor of the Clarion. Blatchford signed himself Nunquam. He dedicates the book to his son. He opens by adopting the insult thrown at him. Infidel stands printed in capitals. It is his new name, and he wants to get used to it. Christian gentlemen bestowed it as a reproach; to his ears the word sounds almost pleasant.

Walking the Strand with his black pipe, Blatchford sets out his case. He argues against the Christian God of his upbringing. Suffering, eternal punishment, and the churches' conduct toward the poor are his counts. He writes as a demagogue and owns that too. His prose is plain and meant for working readers. The book made him Britain's most argued with unbeliever.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BreedenArthur_B:
On April 2, 1964, Special Agent Richard Boyd Smith of the FBI's St. Louis office filed this report on Lee Harvey Oswald. It carries the character Internal Security — R — Cuba, file SL 105-3665, part of the Bureau's security file on the accused assassin.

The report was opened after a letter from Mrs. Faye Breeden of Union, Missouri, one of thousands of citizens whose tips and claims the Bureau logged after the assassination. Each such report chased a single thread and closed it or passed it on. This one is preserved as part of the vast paper wake Oswald left in FBI files across the country.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CubanBoatSeizur:
Marilyn Berger reported for the Washington Post on a fresh round of denials from the State Department. The United States again said it had no role in Cuban boat seizures and no part in plans to attack Cuba. The denials followed the seizure of the Johnny Express by Cuban exiles.

Berger's article catches Washington managing a familiar problem. Exile groups acted against Cuba on their own, while the government insisted in public that it was not behind them. Each new seizure forced the same denial to be issued again, and her report records one of those rounds in full.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MillerArthur_Mi:
An unidentified writer sent this letter on August 29, 1968, to the playwright Arthur Miller. Miller's address is given as Tophet Road in Roxbury, Connecticut. The letter rebukes Miller and other intellectuals for staying silent. It says their silence came as 'the end of the democratic process' was being formalized.

The summer of 1968 gave such a letter plenty of fuel: assassinations, a war, and a violent party convention. The writer demands that famous names speak. Whether Miller answered is not in the file. What survives is the accusation itself, in the plain form of a citizen's letter to a public man, preserved because someone kept it with the era's political papers.
in-the-court-of-king-arthur:
Samuel E. Lowe's In the Court of King Arthur is a children's retelling of Arthurian legend, following a boy named Allan into Camelot and the world of the Round Table. An opening chapter asks who King Arthur was, noting that the stories are probably not strict history even if a real British king may stand behind them.

Allan finds a champion, meets Merlin, watches tournaments, and crosses paths with Tristram, Launcelot and Galahad as the tale moves toward the quest for the Grail. Chapters on King Mark's foul plan, the rescue of captives and the journey home keep the adventures brisk and self-contained. The book offers young readers a friendly doorway into the knights, quests and enchantments of the Arthurian cycle.
lady-larkspur:
Meredith Nicholson published Lady Larkspur with Scribner's in 1919. It first ran as a serial in 1918. Nicholson dedicated it to Bennett and Peggy Gates.

Only five chapter titles appear in this contents list. They promise troops, an amazing widow, a fan, pursuing knights, and Alice. The short list hints at a light, theatrical plot. A widow's arrival seems to set the action moving. Nicholson writes brisk social comedy here, aimed at readers who enjoy wit, disguise, and romance. The brevity of the contents hints at a single swift plot. Nicholson favors charm and pace over heavy moral weight here.
le-petit-nord-or-annals-of-a-labrador-ha:
Anne Grenfell wrote Le Petit Nord as annals of a Labrador harbour. The Grenfell name links the book to medical mission work in Labrador. Its transcriber kept the original dialect and odd spellings.

Annals follow the seasons of a small northern port. Fishing, weather, sickness, and travel shape daily life there. Local speech gives the record a vivid, lived feel. Grenfell writes from close knowledge of the coast and its people. The book preserves a remote community's year in affectionate detail. Harbour life here means boats, ice, and long isolation. Grenfell's annals honor endurance more than adventure.
letters-of-the-right-honourable-lady-m-y:
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's letters were written during her husband's embassy to Turkey. A new edition, complete in one volume, appeared in London in 1790. Its title promises accounts of Turkish policy and manners.

A preface by a lady, written in 1724, introduces the book. She claims the author saw sources closed to other travelers. Inside, courts, harems, baths, and smallpox inoculation receive vivid treatment. Montagu's Turkish letters changed how Britain pictured the Ottoman world. Her wit and curiosity still carry every page. Her praise of Turkish women's freedom startled English readers. Smallpox inoculation, which she championed, saved many later lives.
m-or-n-similia-similibus-curantur:
M. or N. is a novel by G. J. Whyte-Melville, the sporting writer. Its motto, 'Similia similibus curantur,' means like cures like. An early picture shows police arriving at a tense moment. Chapters bring in Tom Ryfe and a burglar known as Gentleman Jim.

A lady named Nina and the young Dick Stanmore carry the love interest. The officers' mess adds soldiers and their talk to the mix. 'Missing — A Gentleman' and 'Wanted — A Lady' promise mystery and pursuit. Whyte-Melville mixes crime, sport, and society in his easy style. The book is a brisk Victorian tale of rogues and respectability. Its title's riddle is part of the game.
mr-sponge-s-sporting-tour:
Robert Smith Surtees wrote this comic sporting novel about Mr. Sponge. Sponge, called Soapey by friends, loves hunting and horses. The book is dedicated to Lord Elcho, a famed Border huntsman. Chapter one finds Sponge walking Oxford Street on a murky day.

Surtees follows Sponge on tour among rich hosts and hunt fields. Sponge lives by his wits and other men's stables. Hosts want sport, while Sponge wants free keep and fun. The jokes turn on class, horses, and sham pride. It remains a classic of English hunting humor, sharp about men who live for the chase.
my-friend-the-chauffeur:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote this motoring novel, issued in 1905. The Williamsons had written The Lightning Conductor, a famed car tale. Ralph Moray tells the first half in chapters of surprises. Each chapter is named for plans, revenges, or mishaps.

Beechy Kidder tells the second half in her own voice. Her chapters promise dolls, thrills, and brakes and worms. Cars were new and thrilling when this book came out. A chauffeur friend drives the plot and the romance. The tale mixes travel, class, and love on early roads, told with speed and a light, teasing touch.
nasa-tm-19670015291-experimental-study-o:
Roland C. Fisher, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, studied a piece of space power hardware in this report. His subject is a mercury-vapor condenser, cooled by gas flowing across a single tube. Mercury vapor systems were then candidates for generating power in space.

Fisher cycled the inlet vapor flow and watched two responses. He tracked the condenser inlet pressure and the position of the liquid-vapor boundary. The condenser showed two distinct regions of operation, with different pressure behavior in each. Results were presented as frequency response plots over a slow cycling range, with an overdamped response for the boundary motion.
nasa-tm-19680011798-computer-code-for-ca:
Ronald L. Danilowicz, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, wrote this memorandum in April 1968. It presents a computer code for calculating temperature profiles in a propellant tank. Tank walls heat and cool unevenly, and the fuel inside follows its own temperature history.

The code is written in FORTRAN IV, the era's standard engineering language. It determines temperature histories in the tank from wall heating and internal heating together. Danilowicz explains the analysis the code rests on. Engineers could then predict hot and cold spots in a tank before metal was cut.
nasa-tm-19680026145-subsonic-longitudina:
Arvo A. Luoma, Richard J. Re, and Donald L. Loving of Langley Research Center compared one transport model in two wind tunnels for this 1968 report. A five-foot-span model of a large subsonic cargo transport ran in both the Langley 8-foot and 16-foot transonic tunnels. Test conditions and data methods matched between the two runs.

Agreement between the tunnels was generally satisfactory. The largest differences appeared at lift coefficients beyond cruise lift. Unequal flow separation effects at supercritical speeds probably explain those gaps. The authors conclude that large-span models can be tested in slotted tunnels with confidence. That confidence holds when test techniques and data reduction follow accepted standards.
nasa-tm-19690023308-the-evaluation-of-tr:
Bobby G. Junkin of Marshall Space Flight Center evaluates tracking errors from the first three Apollo-Saturn V flights in this May 1969 report. The flights were AS-501, AS-502, and AS-503. A truncated TEMS error model was fitted to each flight's tracking data.

Error model coefficient spreads stayed fairly stable from radar to radar. One exception appeared in azimuth and elevation servo-lag coefficients for the Bermuda and Grand Bahama radars. Servo-lag errors and range scale and timing errors occurred frequently in the models. Azimuth nonparallelism and nonperpendicularity terms occurred only rarely. Junkin finds supporting evidence that the truncated model approach yields valid, realistic error models.
nasa-tm-19700022695-deposition-of-alloy-:
Talivaldis Spalvins of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in June 1970. It describes a new way to lay alloy films on complex surfaces. The method joins two known processes, ion plating and flash evaporation, into one.

Spalvins calls the combined method IPFE. It can deposit an alloy film without changing the alloy's makeup, he reports. He coated three alloys in the tests, and checks showed each kept its starting mix. The films could coat hard shapes, into cavities and around corners, on a fixed part. He also reports that the bond of the films was exceptionally strong.
nasa-tm-19700031491-use-of-the-computer-:
L. P. Ludwig, J. Zuk, and R. L. Johnson of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an October 1970 fluid power meeting in Chicago. It shows how computers served in the design of gas turbine mainshaft seals. The seals had to work at shaft surface speeds far beyond past practice.

The team programmed analyses of the seal's temperature field, bending, and force balance. They ran the analyses again and again to settle on a final design. At high speed, heat, and pressure, the sealing faces must not rub, they note. Self-acting lift pads hold the faces apart on a thin gas film.
nasa-tm-19720005767-saturn-component-fai:
The Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory at the Marshall Space Flight Center issued this handbook in 1971, as NASA TM X-64619. It runs to sixty three pages. The subject is failure rates for Saturn rocket components. Reliability engineers needed shared numbers to predict how often parts would fail. The Saturn program's size made guesswork especially risky.

The book gives failure rates for families of mechanical and electromechanical parts. It also gives failure mode frequency ratios, which show how each part tends to fail. Environmental adjustment factors let users adapt the rates to harsher or gentler settings. The values came from a series of studies. Their purpose was to serve design, testing, and reliability work across the program.
our-saviour:
Father Tuck's Our Saviour is a Victorian picture-book life of Jesus for children, retelling the New Testament in simple, stately prose. It opens with John the Baptist preaching at the Jordan. All Judea and Jerusalem come to be baptized there. John warns that one much greater follows him, who will baptize with the Holy Ghost.

Jesus comes from Nazareth and insists on baptism; the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice names him the beloved Son. Then come the forty days of temptation in the wilderness. Jesus resists them with his Father's help. The calling of Simon Peter and Andrew beside the Sea of Galilee follows. They are to be fishers of men. Raphael Tuck's series dressed Bible stories in chromolithographs for the nursery shelf.
peter-ruff-and-the-double-four: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of Peter Ruff and the Double Four, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names E. Phillips Oppenheim. The contents divide the book in two: a first book introducing Mr. Peter Ruff, his new career, Vincent Cawdor the commission agent, and the demand of the Double-Four. A second book recalling Ruff, with an ambassador's wife, seven suppers, and the man behind the curtain.
primitive-christian-worship-or-the-evide:
J. Endell Tyler, rector of St. Giles-in-the-Fields and canon residentiary of St. Paul's, published the second edition of his Primitive Christian Worship in London in 1847, printed for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. The subtitle states the brief: the testimony of holy Scripture and the church, against the invocation of saints and angels and the Blessed Virgin Mary. Two texts stand as epigraphs and rules of engagement: speaking the truth in love, and prove all things, hold fast that which is good.

Tyler writes amid the Oxford Movement, when early church practice was evidence in a live trial between Canterbury and Rome. His method is cumulative testimony: what the first Christians did not do, he argues, the church may not command. The book reached a second edition because the argument was current coin.
reason-and-faith-their-claims-and-confli:
Henry Rogers took up the claims of reason and faith in the Edinburgh Review for October 1849, in volume 90 of that journal. His essay reviews three books: Historic Doubts relative to Napoleon Buonaparte, J. A. Froude's Nemesis of Faith, and F. J. Foxton's Popular Christianity. The piece runs from page 293 to page 356.

Rogers rejects the old saying that reason is the firstborn while faith inherits the blessing. Men trust and believe, he argues, long before they reason, yet the two grow together in human nature. Neither can shut out the other, and the faith approved in the New Testament is not faith without reason. Christians, he notes, are told to give a reason for their hope.
six-feet-four:
Jackson Gregory published this western tale in 1917 and gave the book to E. M. Gregory with a plain note: here's your book. Contents open in a storm on a devil's own night, then name Buck Thornton, a man's man. A ford, a man from Poison Hole Ranch, and Winifred judging a man follow.

Later heads promise a double theft, moonlight, the Bedloe boys, and Rattlesnake Pollard. A dance at the Deer Creek schoolhouse waits down the list. Gregory writes the tall-hero western in classic form: a six-foot-four stranger, ranch feuds, and a woman whose verdict on a man matters most.
sonnets-by-the-nawab-nizamat-jung-bahadu: Sonnets by the Nawab Nizamat Jung Bahadur is dated 1917. Two mottos on love open the book. Empedocles is quoted on the soul and the eye. Love, he says, is found by the soul alone. Plato is quoted on the Divine. Beauty, wisdom, and goodness feed the soul's wings. The contents list a foreword by R. C. Fraser. A note on the sonnet's past in English letters follows. A prologue stands before the sonnets. Rebirth, The Crown of Life, and Before the Throne lead them.
supreme-personality-fun-in-living-a-doub:
Dr. Delmer Eugene Croft, a psychotherapist and lecturer, wrote Supreme Personality as a course of lessons billed on its cover as Fun in Living, a doubt, fear, and worry cure. The booklet sold for twenty-five cents and boasted a printing in the one hundredth thousand.

Its cover lines set the tone. A man should be grander at eighty than at eighteen. Worry builds no happy home. A religion that makes you miserable should be traded in. A happy philosophy should take its place. Inside, Croft teaches that personality rests on self-consciousness with self-governed intelligence and self-directed action. The lessons promise to kill doubt, fear, and worry, cure the habit of growing old, and pipe the reader into the power house of the universe.
tacitus-and-bracciolini-the-annals-forge:
John Wilson Ross's Tacitus and Bracciolini argues a bold charge in its very title: The Annals Forged in the Fifteenth Century. The book was first published anonymously at London in 1878, and Ross dedicates it to his brother Robert.

Ross lays the blame on Poggio Bracciolini, the great Italian finder of lost classics, quoting Paolo Cortese on Poggio's matchless skill at imitation and his drive to copy any style he admired. Latin epigraphs from admirers and critics crowd the front pages. The book belongs to the long quarrel over forged and genuine antiques. Ross holds a clear position in it. The Annals of Tacitus, as the world had them, were a Renaissance fabrication. They were not a work of imperial Rome.
the-alleged-haunting-of-b-house-includin: Only the opening pages are present: the title page of a London book from 1899, printed by George Redway. Floor-plan plates show attics, upper floors, ground floor, and basement. The work pairs a journal kept while Colonel Lemesurier Taylor held the tenancy of the house with editing by A. Goodrich-Freer, styled Miss X, and John, Marquess of Bute. A quoted note from Frederic W. H. Myers of the Society for Psychical Research cites The Times of June 10, 1897. It doubts that proof fit for the Society's Proceedings had been found.
the-amateur:
Richard Harding Davis opens this tale aboard a ship in thick February weather off the Banks. Austin Ford, star reporter for the New York Republic, rides out a blizzard in the smoking room. He is bound for England to serve as the paper's London man, though he protests that his real work lies at home.

Ford hunts a sharp class of crook: the cashier who hides theft with new tricks, the dishonest company head, the con man whose only weapon is wit. Davis makes clear Ford loathes the label amateur detective. He sees his job as warning the public about bad men, then letting readers judge their fate.
the-chink-in-the-armour: Mrs. Belloc Lowndes, author of The Lodger, wrote this novel, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1912. Only the title page, a Spectator quotation used as an epigraph, and a bare list of chapter numbers are present here. The epigraph holds that society runs on the assumption that murder will not be committed, and calls that assumption the one chink in its chain armour.Past that front matter, the record is silent.
the-lost-gospel-and-its-contents-or-the-:
The Rev. M. F. Sadler, rector of Honiton, published The Lost Gospel and Its Contents in London in 1876. Its subtitle announces the method: the author of Supernatural Religion refuted by himself. Sadler explains in his preface that the book he answers tried to discredit the supernatural element of Christianity. Its claim was that second-century writers quoted earlier, lost Gospels in place of the present ones. Sadler turns that claim around.

If the early writers did quote earlier narratives, he argues, those narratives contained substantially the same Gospel now possessed, in a form, if anything, more suggestive of the supernatural. The anonymous author's success would only prove the written Gospel fifty or sixty years older than he allows. Much of the book then examines Justin Martyr's writings closely.
the-louisa-alcott-reader-a-supplementary:
The Louisa Alcott Reader is a supplementary reader for the fourth year of school, gathering ten short pieces by Louisa M. Alcott. The contents mix tales and verses: A Christmas Dream, The Candy Country, Naughty Jocko, The Skipping Shoes, Cockyloo, Rosy's Journey, The Fairy Box, and The Piggy Girl among them. Illustrations show a child named Lily rocking and eating her way through the top of a little tree.

The first piece opens two days before Christmas. Effie, a discontented-looking little girl, watches her mother arrange a pile of gifts and declares she is so tired of Christmas she wishes there never would be another one. Her mother answers that she is as bad as old Scrooge, and warns that something may happen to her, as it did to him.
the-motor-girls-on-a-tour:
Only a series advertisement and a contents list are present here for The Motor Girls on a Tour by Margaret Penrose, so the tour itself does not appear. The advertisement presents The Motor Girls series as a girls' answer to the successful Motor Boys series by Clarence Young. Penrose, it says, is both an able writer and an expert automobilist, and the volumes sell at 75 cents each, postpaid.

Sixteen chapters are listed. A Spoiled Dinner and The Woodland Conference open the book, followed by No Boys! and The Strange Promise. A hold-up, a girl in the ditch, a visit to a grotto, and a lost promise book carry the visible list to A Strange Message at Chapter XVI.
the-past-condition-of-organic-nature-lec:
Thomas H. Huxley delivered The Past Condition of Organic Nature as the second of six lectures to working men at the Museum of Practical Geology in 1863, on Darwin's Origin of Species. Huxley sums up his first lecture: the many forms of animal life reduce to a few primitive plans, and at last to a single cell.

He recalls the great circulation of matter. Plants draw elements from the inorganic world and combine them into food. Animals take plant matter for nourishment and return waste to the inorganic world, and their bodies dissolve back at death. Blade of grass and horse hold the same elements, differently arranged. The lecture builds a plain man's picture of nature's economy.
the-poems-and-prose-of-ernest-dowson-wit: The Poems and Prose of Ernest Dowson opens with a memoir by Arthur Symons. Here only the title page and the start of the contents appear, so the poems and prose themselves are absent. After the memoir come a prefatory poem for Adelaide, a coronal, and a verses section. Titles there include Nuns of the Perpetual Adoration, Villanelle of Sunset, My Lady April, and To One in Bedlam. A Latin-titled piece begins Non sum qualis eram. Later entries name Vanitas, Exile, Spleen, April Love, and A Requiem.
the-prairie-farmer-vol-56-no-2-january-1: Prairie Farmer, a weekly journal for the farm, orchard, and fireside, is shown here in its issue of Saturday, January 12, 1884, printed at Chicago. The paper was established in 1841, and this number is volume 56, number 2, priced at two dollars a year. The pages shown hold the masthead and the moved-up contents list for the number. Agriculture items include dew and soil moisture, specialty in farming, and farm names. Live stock, the dairy, veterinary answers, and horticulture follow. Poultry notes and a piece on the Star of Bethlehem close the list.
the-relation-of-the-hro-lfs-saga-kraka-a: Oscar Ludvig Olson submitted his study at Chicago in 1916. It was his doctoral dissertation in English. He compares an Icelandic saga with Beowulf. He compares a set of ballad verses with it too. The work traces saga growth in two lands. England and the Scandinavian countries both figure in it. Only the title pages are present here. The opening of the bibliography appears with them. An abbreviations list begins there as well. The argument itself does not appear.
the-sceptics-of-the-old-testament-job-ko:
E. J. Dillon wrote The Sceptics of the Old Testament, treating Job, Koheleth, and Agur. His title page lists many honours. He was late professor at the Imperial University of Kharkoff. He also belonged to the Armenian Academy of Venice and the Société Asiatique de Paris. The volume offers English text translated from the primitive Hebrew. That Hebrew was restored on the basis of recent philological discoveries, the title claims.

Dillon dedicates the pages to Alexander Vassilievitch Paschkoff. His dedicatory note recalls sixteen years of discussions with Paschkoff. Three conversations stand engraven in his memory, he writes. The first took place in St. Petersburg one Indian-summer evening. They looked from the Gagarine Quay over the Neva. Its waters reflected the gold of the Fortress church spire. A second talk came nine years later, on the ice-bound river in December cold.
the-sign-of-the-four:
Arthur Conan Doyle's The Sign of the Four runs to twelve chapters, its contents say. The science of deduction opens the book. The statement of the case and the tragedy of Pondicherry Lodge follow. Sherlock Holmes gives a demonstration at chapter six. The Baker Street Irregulars, the great Agra treasure, and Jonathan Small's story close the list.

Chapter one finds Holmes at his hypodermic syringe. He takes the bottle from the mantel-piece corner, Watson narrates. With long, nervous fingers he adjusts the needle and bares his forearm. The forearm is dotted and scarred with innumerable puncture-marks, Watson notes. Holmes sinks back with a long sigh of satisfaction. Watson has witnessed this performance three times a day for months. Custom has not reconciled him to it, he confesses.
the-wouldbegoods-being-the-further-adven:
E. Nesbit's The Wouldbegoods continues the adventures of the Bastable treasure seekers. She dedicates the book to her son Fabian Bland. Fourteen chapters promise a jungle, a circus, and Canterbury pilgrims. Chapter one opens with the children's Indian uncle. He compares children to jam, pleasant in the right place only. The young narrator reports feeling both young and angry.

The children cannot simply dismiss him as nasty. Their uncle, they admit, is usually the opposite. Calling jam nice hardly counts as an insult either. Nesbit's humor grows from such honest child logic. Readers get schemes by well-meaning children determined to be good. Their good intentions reliably produce chaos.
tom-swift-and-his-air-glider-or-seeking-: Seeking the Platinum Treasure takes Tom Swift toward Siberia in the air glider story by Victor Appleton, opening with a contents list of twenty-five chapters. Headings promise a breakdown, a daring project, the hand of the Czar, rescuing Mr. Petrofsky, spies, a Russian prison, and a lost salt mine. Siberia is the goal. Chapter one, A Breakdown, starts with Tom asking whether Ned is ready, then breaks off. The contents and that line are present here, so the Russian adventure itself does not appear beyond them.
